title: Lot's wife looks back (Genesis 19)
hookLine: the cities fall, and a woman with no name turns to look
tomorrow: hagar and ishmael in the desert

lines: A CITY TURNS ON ITS GUESTS.
cards: Two of the travelers reach Sodom at evening. Lot is sitting at the city gate, and like his uncle, he jumps up, bows, and brings them home to eat.
But that night the men of the city surround the house and demand the strangers be handed over. It's the opposite of Abraham's open tent: a city that turns on its guests.
The visitors strike the mob blind and tell Lot: get your family out; this place is about to be destroyed. At dawn, Lot is still there. He lingered, the Torah says, dragging his feet.
So the angels grab him, his wife and his two daughters by the hand, and pull them out. Run for your life, they say. Don't look back.

teach.b: Fire and sulfur rain down on Sodom and Gomorrah. Then, in the old JPS translation: "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt." That's all we're told.
She has no name in the Torah, and we never hear her say a word. Later tradition named her Edit, and the rabbis asked: why did she look? One old midrash answers with compassion.
Some of her daughters were married and still in the city, and she turned to see whether they were following: a mother looking for her children. Another midrash, cited by Rashi, is sharper.
When Lot brought the guests home, she wouldn't give them even salt for their food, and so she became salt.
That ties her to the city's real sin, which in rabbinic tradition is cruelty. The prophet Ezekiel describes Sodom as proud and full of bread, living at ease, never helping the poor and needy.
The Talmud tells stories of Sodom's laws against strangers and against charity.

teach.h: SHE LOOKED BACK FROM BEHIND HIM.
teach.b: Maybe looking back means you can't be rescued from a place while your heart is still living there. Lot dragged his feet. His wife turned around.
Read that way, the story doesn't mock her; it grieves. And near the Dead Sea today, on the salt cliffs of Mount Sodom, there's a pillar of rock that people call Lot's wife.

how: Jews read the destruction of Sodom in the Torah portion Vayera; rabbinic tradition teaches that Sodom's sin was cruelty to strangers and the poor, and teachers often pair the story with Ezekiel's description of the city.

o: she turned toward the city and became salt

s: the Torah tells us the name of Lot's wife
she has no name and no words in the Torah. later tradition calls her Edit.
rabbinic tradition sees Sodom's sin as cruelty to strangers and the poor
Ezekiel says it never helped the poor and needy; the Talmud tells of its laws against strangers.
in one midrash, she looked back to see if her daughters were following
some of her daughters had stayed in the city, married. a mother looking for her children.

games.q: you're running from the burning city. the angels said, don't look back. behind you, you hear it falling. what do you do?
games.why: Lot's wife looks back from behind him and becomes a pillar of salt. the Torah gives no reason; the midrash imagines she was looking for her daughters.

practice: Think of one thing you keep looking back at: an old argument you replay, a job you didn't get, a version of your life that ended.
Looking back is human, and it can be love, like a mother looking for her daughters; but notice if it's keeping you frozen, thank it for what it was, then picture turning your face forward.
If you pray, you can ask for help letting go.

wordCard.voice: Lot's wife looks back. A woman with no name, rescued by the hand, who turned toward the burning city and became a pillar of salt.

carryVoice: Your line: face forward. She was rescued by the hand, and still she turned. That's day forty-six.
